body:
Why Cities Required Special Administration

A large city brought together officials, soldiers, merchants, artisans, labourers and visitors. It needed arrangements for trade, supplies, the movement of people, the recording of information and the collection of revenue.

Pataliputra served as the Mauryan capital and an important urban centre. Megasthenes described it as a large city with substantial fortifications. According to his account, its surrounding wall had 570 towers and 64 gates. These figures are part of the surviving Greek description and should be understood as reported figures rather than independently verified measurements.

The 30-Member Municipal Administration

Megasthenes described an urban administrative body containing 30 members divided into 6 committees of 5 members each. Each committee dealt with a different aspect of city life.

The committees were responsible for the following:

  1. Industries and crafts: Supervision of artisans and industrial activities.
  2. Foreign visitors: Arrangements concerning the stay, needs and movement of foreigners.
  3. Births and deaths: Registration and maintenance of relevant population records.
  4. Trade: Supervision of markets, commercial transactions, weights and measures.
  5. Manufactured goods: Inspection and regulation of goods offered for sale, including concerns about mixing old and new products.
  6. Sales tax: Collection of revenue on goods sold in the city.

Megasthenes' account reports a levy of one-tenth of the value of goods sold. This figure should not be confused with the agricultural share of produce or treated as proof of a single sales-tax rate throughout the entire empire.

How the Committees Worked Together

The committees had different responsibilities, but city administration required coordination.

For example, when goods were brought to an urban market, the authorities needed to monitor commercial practices, check the use of weights and measures, oversee the goods offered for sale and collect applicable duties. When traders arrived from distant regions, the administration also had to deal with visitors and their requirements.

The registration of births and deaths was another administrative responsibility. Such information could help the government understand the population living under its authority.

The Nagaraka in the Arthashastra

The Arthashastra describes a city superintendent called the nagaraka. It also discusses subordinate officers concerned with neighbourhoods, households and records.

The titles and arrangement described in the Arthashastra should be distinguished from Megasthenes' account of the 6 municipal committees. Both sources are useful for understanding ancient ideas about urban government, but they do not establish that an identical administrative structure operated in every Mauryan town.

Urban Administration and Provincial Administration Are Different

Provincial administration concerned the government of large territories and the implementation of imperial instructions across regions.

Urban administration concerned the everyday management of a particular city, including markets, occupations, records and municipal revenue.

A provincial governor could supervise a broad region containing several towns and villages. A municipal body dealt with specific functions within a city. These are related but different levels of government.

Prelims focus

  • Megasthenes described 30 municipal officers at Pataliputra.
  • They were organised into 6 committees of 5 members each.
  • The committees dealt with crafts, foreigners, births and deaths, trade, manufactured goods and sales taxation.
  • Megasthenes reported a tax of one-tenth on goods sold.
  • Nagaraka refers to a city superintendent in the Arthashastra.
  • Trap: The 6 municipal committees were different from the 6 military subcommittees also described by Megasthenes.

[Sources: Megasthenes' account of Pataliputra as preserved in later Greek accounts; IGNOU, 'Economy of the Mauryan Period', Unit 19, section on urban administration, crafts and commerce; Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book II, Chapter 36, 'The Duties of a City Superintendent', R. Shamasastry translation, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed p. 78.]

pictures.caption: Megasthenes described 30 municipal officers working in 6 committees.

title: Urban Administration: Pataliputra and the Municipal Committees

body:
Why the Army Was Essential to the Empire

A large empire needed armed forces to defend its territory, protect communication routes and support the authority of its rulers. The Mauryas controlled regions separated by great distances, so military power depended not only on fighting soldiers but also on transport and regular supplies.

Maintaining soldiers and animals required food, fodder, equipment, trained workers and revenue. The army therefore depended on the agricultural economy and the administrative machinery that collected and distributed resources.

The Four Traditional Fighting Arms

The ancient Indian expression chaturanga refers to the 4 principal fighting arms of an army:

  • Infantry: Soldiers fighting on foot.
  • Cavalry: Soldiers mounted on horses.
  • Chariots: Horse-drawn vehicles used in warfare.
  • Elephants: War elephants used as a distinctive component of ancient Indian armies.

These were fighting formations. Military administration, however, also required arrangements for transport, supplies and other supporting activities.

Megasthenes' Six Military Subcommittees

Megasthenes described a committee divided into 6 subcommittees for organising military affairs:

  1. Navy.
  2. Transport and provisions.
  3. Infantry.
  4. Cavalry.
  5. Chariots.
  6. Elephants.

The transport and provisions subcommittee had especially varied responsibilities. It arranged vehicles for equipment, food for soldiers, fodder for animals and workers who maintained the equipment and attended to the army.

Remember the distinction: Chaturanga identifies 4 fighting arms. Megasthenes' account identifies 6 military subcommittees because it also includes the navy and transport with provisions.

How Large Was the Mauryan Army?

Greek accounts report that the Mauryan rulers maintained an army containing approximately 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants.

These are figures reported in ancient Greek accounts. They should not be presented as independently confirmed military statistics. Historians have questioned their reliability and consider that some numbers may have been exaggerated.

The main historical conclusion is that the Mauryan state possessed substantial military resources and required a system capable of maintaining and supplying them.

Communications and the Movement of Officials

Roads, rivers and messengers connected the capital with provincial centres. Maintaining these connections was essential because orders, reports, resources and military reinforcements had to move across long distances.

Taxila and Ujjayini were important partly because they lay on major routes. The choice of these administrative centres therefore served both political and economic purposes.

The Intelligence System

The Arthashastra gives considerable importance to intelligence gathering. It uses the term gudhapurusha for a secret agent and describes different forms of intelligence activity.

Two broad categories commonly identified in accounts of its intelligence system are:

  • Samstha: Agents operating from a relatively fixed position or establishment.
  • Sanchara: Agents who moved from place to place.

The purpose was to obtain information that ordinary official reporting might fail to reveal. Intelligence could help the ruler learn about threats, local conditions and the conduct of government officers.

The general use of spies to watch officials is also described in the account of Mauryan government presented in NCERT. Nevertheless, the detailed arrangements recommended in the Arthashastra should not be assumed to have been implemented in exactly the same form across the empire.

Information Reaching the Emperor

Ashoka's Major Rock Edict VI refers to arrangements for reports on public affairs to reach the emperor at different times and places. This provides direct inscriptional evidence that communication and the disposal of public business were treated as important royal duties.

Official reports and secret intelligence were not identical. Officials transmitted information through administrative channels, while the intelligence system described in the Arthashastra sought information through agents operating less openly.

Prelims focus

  • Chaturanga refers to infantry, cavalry, chariots and elephants.
  • Megasthenes described 6 military subcommittees.
  • The 6 subcommittees included the navy and transport with provisions.
  • Samstha refers to stationary intelligence arrangements; sanchara refers to moving agents.
  • Major Rock Edict VI concerns the reporting of public affairs to Ashoka.
  • Trap: The large army figures reported by Greek writers are historical claims, not independently verified counts.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed pp. 34–35; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed pp. 77–78; IGNOU, 'Administrative and Institutional Structures', Unit 24, section 24.4; Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book I, chapters on secret agents, R. Shamasastry translation, consulted 18 November 2026; Ashoka, Major Rock Edict VI, E. Hultzsch translation, Inscriptions of Asoka, 1925, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Megasthenes’ 6 military subcommittees include the 4 Chaturanga fighting arms, navy, and transport and provisions, which supplies the forces.
pictures.caption: Military organisation combined fighting forces with transport and supplies.

pictures.alt: Official reports and Arthashastra intelligence both inform the emperor; secret agents are grouped as relatively stationary Samstha and moving Sanchara.
pictures.caption: Official reports and intelligence supplied different kinds of information to the ruler.

title: The Mauryan Army, Communications and Intelligence System

body:
Why the Mauryan State Needed Revenue

The Mauryan Empire required resources for its army, officials, administrative centres, roads and other public activities. These resources came from agriculture, trade, productive activities and the control of valuable natural resources.

Revenue could be collected in different forms. Agricultural produce could be received in kind, while some payments were made in money. The system therefore involved both the collection of goods and the management of monetary resources.

Because the empire contained different regions and economic activities, all revenue should not be understood as a single land tax.

Agricultural Revenue and Bhaga

Bhaga means a share of agricultural produce claimed as revenue by the ruler. In ancient Indian political and legal traditions, one-sixth of the produce is a commonly mentioned normal share.

For example, if a cultivator produced 600 units of grain and the applicable share was one-sixth, the ruler's share would be 100 units. This illustrates the meaning of the fraction; it does not establish that every Mauryan cultivator paid exactly this rate.

Actual obligations could vary with locality, the nature of cultivation, the status of the land and special royal orders. The evidence does not justify applying a uniform one-sixth rate to every field throughout the empire.

Important Revenue Terms

TermBasic meaningDistinction
BhagaRuler's share of agricultural produce.Linked specifically to agricultural output.
BaliA customary levy or contribution.Not identical to the agricultural share called bhaga.
HiranyaA term associated with payments in money or cash dues.Its precise use depended on the context.
ShulkaTolls or customs duties connected with trade.Collected from commercial movement or transactions.
SitaLand or agricultural production directly associated with the state.State-managed production rather than a tax on an independent cultivator.
VishtiLabour demanded as an obligation.A labour service rather than an ordinary monetary payment.

These terms occur in ancient textual and inscriptional evidence. Some refer to taxes, some to productive assets and others to obligations. Treating them all as interchangeable types of land revenue would be inaccurate.

Tax and Tribute Are Not the Same

Tax generally refers to a levy collected in accordance with an established obligation, often at regular intervals.

Tribute refers to resources obtained from a community or subordinate authority when such collection was possible or expected. It did not necessarily follow the same regular assessment and collection arrangements as agricultural taxation.

For example, cultivators in areas under more direct administration could pay an assessed share of produce. More distant communities might supply valuable goods or materials as tribute.

Revenue Beyond Agriculture

The Arthashastra describes the importance of resources obtained from several activities:

  • State-managed agriculture: Production from lands cultivated under government supervision.
  • Mines and minerals: Valuable materials required for tools, weapons and other products.
  • Forests: Timber, elephants and other forest resources.
  • Trade: Duties on goods and commercial movement.
  • Pastures and other productive resources: Economic activities that could contribute to state income.

The attention given to these activities shows that the Mauryan state was concerned not only with taxation but also with protecting and supervising sources of production.

Samaharta and Sannidhata

Two offices are especially useful for understanding the difference between collecting revenue and managing what had been collected.

The Samaharta was the chief officer concerned with revenue assessment and collection. The Sannidhata was concerned with the custody, accounting and storage of treasury resources and state stores.

The distinction is practical: one function brings revenue into the government's possession; the other safeguards and accounts for it.

A Recorded Exception: Lumbini

The Rummindei or Lumbini pillar inscription provides an important example of a special fiscal concession.

It records that Ashoka visited Lumbini, the birthplace of the Buddha, in his 20th year after coronation. The inscription is commonly interpreted as stating that the village was released from the levy called bali and that its share of produce was reduced to one-eighth.

This is an important distinction. The inscription does not simply establish that Lumbini was exempted from every possible agricultural obligation. Its wording records a special concession involving the levy and the share of produce.

One-sixth and one-eighth refer to different circumstances. One-sixth is a commonly stated agricultural share in ancient texts. One-eighth is the special reduced share traditionally understood from the Lumbini inscription.

Revenue and State Expenditure

Revenue made it possible to pay officials, maintain military forces, support administration and undertake certain public works. At the same time, these activities could protect productive land, communication routes and markets, helping the state preserve the economic resources from which future revenue was obtained.

Prelims focus

  • Bhaga refers to the ruler's share of agricultural produce.
  • One-sixth is a commonly mentioned normal share in ancient Indian texts, not a proven universal Mauryan rate.
  • Shulka refers to trade-related tolls or customs duties.
  • Samaharta was associated with revenue collection; Sannidhata with treasury custody.
  • The Lumbini inscription records a special concession commonly understood as exemption from bali and payment of a one-eighth share.
  • Trap: Sita refers to state-managed agricultural land or production, not simply another name for bhaga.

[Sources: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book II, chapters on state lands, departments and revenue collection, R. Shamasastry translation, consulted 18 November 2026; IGNOU, 'Economy of the Mauryan Period', Unit 19, sections 19.2–19.4, printed pp. 21–30; Ashoka, Rummindei or Lumbini pillar inscription, in E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka, 1925, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed pp. 77–78.]

pictures.alt: Six revenue sources flow through Samaharta’s collection and Sannidhata’s treasury custody to state expenditure, as goods or money.
pictures.caption: Different sources of revenue supported the activities of the state.

title: Mauryan Revenue: Land Tax, Trade Duties and the Treasury
